analysis.one_liner: Tightens safety, crime-reporting, and medical rules for cruise ships serving US passengers.
analysis.headline: The Cruise Passenger Protection Act, introduced with 10 cosponsors including 2 Republicans, was referred to a House subcommittee the day after introduction and never received a hearing, a markup, or any vote before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strengthen federal rules for large cruise ships that embark or disembark passengers in the United States. It would require faster reporting of crimes to the FBI and US consulates, video surveillance in common areas with victims able to obtain the footage for lawsuits, a qualified physician on board at all times, defibrillators and CPR-trained crews, peep holes on cabin doors, equipment to detect passengers who fall overboard, and training certified for crew in crime-scene preservation. It would also let the government deny US entry to cruise operators that violate the rules or refuse to pay penalties, and would allow families to recover damages for loss of care, comfort, and companionship when a loved one dies in a cruise accident on the high seas.
analysis.who_benefits: Cruise passengers and their families. The bill targets the safety gaps that matter most to travelers: crimes at sea that go unreported or unpreserved on video, ships without adequate medical staff, and liability limits that currently cut off compensation for families of passengers who die in international waters.

how_it_helps.text: Requires vessel owners to notify the FBI within 4 hours of learning of an alleged crime on board, and to report incidents involving US nationals to the nearest US consulate before the ship departs a US port

Requires video surveillance in every passenger common area, clear signage about it, 30-day retention of footage, 5-year preservation of footage relevant to reported crimes, and gives victims or their legal representatives the right to obtain copies of video records for civil suits

Requires a physician with emergency medicine experience to be present and available at all times, a sufficient medical staff sized to the passenger load, automated external defibrillators throughout the ship, and CPR certification for every crew member
Requires a peep hole in every passenger stateroom and crew cabin door, electronic logging of which crew member enters each stateroom, and technology to detect passengers who have fallen overboard
Allows families to recover nonpecuniary damages — loss of care, comfort, and companionship — for deaths from cruise ship accidents on the high seas beyond 12 nautical miles from US shores

Lets the Department of Homeland Security withhold or revoke a ship's clearance and lets the Coast Guard deny entry to the United States for operators that violate the rules or fail to pay penalties, giving the requirements real teeth

analysis.who_pays: Cruise line operators bear the compliance costs: medical staffing around the clock, video systems and retention, door and deck retrofits, crew training, and expanded liability for deaths at sea. Some of that cost would likely reach passengers through ticket prices.

drawbacks.text: Requires vessel owners to staff a qualified physician at all times and to retrofit stateroom doors, exterior deck railings, and surveillance systems, ongoing costs that would fall on cruise operators and be passed through to ticket prices

Sets a high bar for on-board physicians — at least 3 years of post-registration experience in general and emergency medicine or board certification in emergency, family, or internal medicine — which could be difficult to staff on every voyage
Lets the Secretary of Transportation waive the design and equipment requirements case by case, recording only the justification, which leaves room for the standards to be loosened in practice

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections address documented failure modes of cruising: crimes reported late or not at all, footage lost, inadequate medical care, and families barred from fair compensation for deaths in international waters. The costs are real but targeted — medical staffing, surveillance hardware, retrofits — and proportionate to the size of the industry. The waiver discretion is the weak point. On balance the benefits to passengers outweigh the compliance burden, though the bill would not have solved the underlying jurisdiction problem of foreign-flagged ships.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation Subcommittee, and sat there without a hearing or markup until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Doris Matsui (D-CA), with Reps. Ted Poe (R-TX) and Jim Himes (D-CT), introduced the bill on April 26, 2017
It gained 10 cosponsors, 8 Democrats and 2 Republicans
It was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure on April 26, 2017, and the next day to the Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — was taken before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cruise line operators, which avoided the medical-staffing, surveillance, retrofit, and reporting requirements and the expanded death-at-sea liability the bill would have imposed. Passengers and their families got no new protections.

for.name: Rep. Doris Matsui
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Cruise Passenger Protection Act and sought cosponsors

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Rep. Bill Shuster, R-PA)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation Subcommittee and never scheduled a markup or reported it out

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan — 8 Democrats and 2 Republicans — and there is no recorded opposition or vote in the record; the bill's obstruction happened silently, in committee.

industries.industry: Cruise line operators (large international lines, mostly foreign-flagged)
industries.note: The bill would impose round-the-clock physician staffing, mandatory surveillance with victim access to footage, strict FBI and consulate crime-reporting deadlines, vessel retrofits, and — most costly — recovery of nonpecuniary damages for passenger deaths on the high seas, which current law limits. These are exactly the areas where operators have faced liability for crimes and deaths at sea, so the industry's interest ran against the protections passengers would gain.
Retrofit requirements for peep holes, deck railings, overboard detection technology, and video surveillance systems would have created demand for marine equipment and shipyard work.

industries.industry: Maritime security and medical staffing providers
industries.note: Requirements for on-board physicians, CPR-certified crews, and MARAD-certified crime-scene training would have expanded markets for maritime medical staffing and security training.
